title: IAM Fundamentals
description: Learn about IAM users, groups, roles, MFA, access keys, and security best practices.

data.text: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the service that controls who can access your AWS account and what they are allowed to do. With IAM, you can create individual users, group them, assign permissions, and require multi-factor authentication (MFA) for added security.

data.title: Security First
data.text: AWS recommends never using your root account for daily tasks. Create individual IAM users with the minimum permissions they need.

An IAM user represents a person or service that interacts with AWS. Each user has a name and a set of credentials, such as a password for the AWS Management Console or access keys for the CLI and SDKs.

data.title: User Credentials
items: Password — Used to sign in to the AWS Management Console.
Access Key ID and Secret Access Key — Used by the CLI, SDKs, and API calls.
SSH keys for EC2 — Used to connect to Linux EC2 instances.
Server certificates — Used for HTTPS connections in services like CloudFront.

data.text: An IAM group is a collection of IAM users. Groups make it easier to manage permissions for multiple people at once. For example, you could create a Developers group and give that group access to certain services.
An IAM role is similar to a user but is intended to be assumed by trusted entities. Roles do not have permanent credentials. Instead, they are granted temporary security tokens when assumed.

terms.definition: An identity representing a person or service with long-term credentials.
A collection of IAM users for easier permission management.
An identity with permissions that can be assumed by trusted entities for temporary access.
Multi-Factor Authentication — requires a second form of verification beyond a password.

data.text: MFA adds an extra layer of protection by requiring users to provide two forms of identification. Even if a password is compromised, an attacker cannot access the account without the second factor.

data.title: IAM Best Practices
items: Lock away your root account credentials and do not use them for daily tasks.
Create individual IAM users for each person who needs access.
Use groups to assign permissions to multiple users at once.
Grant least privilege — give users only the permissions they need.
Enable MFA for all users with console access.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: IAM is the service that controls identity and access in AWS
Users represent people or services with long-term credentials
Groups simplify permission management for multiple users
Roles provide temporary access without long-term credentials
MFA adds a critical layer of security to all accounts
data.takeaway: Next, you will learn how IAM policies work in detail.
